title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that evaluated whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) a guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM generation per task shared across arms (model_calls_used = 200; preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. The paper’s principal outcome is methodological and artifact‑grounded: (1) we publish a complete preregistered paired run and analysis; (2) we explain how generation semantics and model‑call budgeting determine testability; and (3) we provide concrete, archive‑grounded recommendations for reproducible repeats with independent per‑arm generation and stronger adversarial coverage. All execution and analysis artifacts cited in this paper are archived (execution/* and analysis/*).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains in network operations (NetOps) but raises safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed configuration change can violate reachability, breach security policy, or trigger outages. Recent work advocates tool‑grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair architectures to reduce such risks. Motivated by those proposals and by calls for workflow‑centred evaluation, we preregistered a confirmatory, paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) to measure whether deterministic verifier augmentation reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals from a hosted LLM under both benign and adversarial prompts.

This paper reports the complete archived run and explains why the preregistered causal test was non‑informative in this execution. The study is not a null endorsement of LLMs or validators; rather, it is an artifact‑anchored methodological report showing how generation semantics, adversarial budgeting, and model‑call accounting interact to determine whether a preregistered paired test can detect verifier benefit. Our contributions are (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on N=200 synthetic NetOps tasks; (2) a precise, artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test yielded no discordant pairs; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations and reproducibility pointers to enable informative repeats.
sections.related_work:
Prior surveys and prototypes document growing interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks—intent translation, configuration synthesis, and automated remediation—and they advocate grounding LLMs with deterministic tools and sandboxed replay to reduce hallucinations and constraint violations [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; IEEE OJCOMS 2026]. Generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine pipelines have demonstrated gains on curated tasks, but observed effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity, prompt design, and generation semantics. Red‑teaming and guardrail research emphasizes safety/utility trade‑offs (false refusals versus unblocked unsafe proposals) and recommends workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations.

Our study follows these prescriptions insofar as it preregistered estimands and sampling, used deterministic synthetic tasks and a deterministic sandboxed validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), archived all model outputs and validator traces, and executed a paired analysis. The novelty here is methodological: publishing a complete confirmatory run that reveals how a particular execution choice (shared_initial_candidate generation semantics) can render the paired causal estimand untestable even when all other parts (task generation, validation, analysis) operate deterministically and reproducibly.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The preregistration (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) defined the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded minus baseline; SAFE encoded as 1). It specified a paired binary design with N=200 unique tasks and planned_episode_count = 400 (two arms per task). The analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) was specified in advance and implemented an exact McNemar two‑sided test with a paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729).

Task generation and adversarial design: A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks under preregistered RNG rules. Tasks targeted constrained, operationally meaningful changes (admin, mtu, vlan fields) across single‑AS, multi‑device topologies and included preregistered adversarial prompt templates (obfuscation and negation transforms). The full task manifest and representative payloads are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

Pipelines and generation semantics: Two pipelines were compared: (a) baseline LLM‑only, and (b) guarded pipeline that pipes the LLM candidate through deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and optionally applies a single automatic repair (preregistered). The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (each pipeline receives an independent LLM call per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM generation shared across arms). The executed run used independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate), so only one LLM call per task occurred and the same candidate was scored in both arms. This execution choice is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini", independent_condition_generation = false) and in the execution manifest (model_calls_used = 200, completed_episode_count = 400).

Model call budgeting and planned alternatives: The preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 to allow independent per‑arm generations. Using shared_initial_candidate reduced model_calls_used to 200 in execution. The preregistration explicitly allowed both semantics and documented the model‑call trade‑offs; we report both the intended budget and the executed usage to make the causal implications explicit.

Deterministic validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation of candidate configurations against the intent and workflow policies; it emitted binary SAFE/UNSAFE labels and detailed validator_traces (validation_before/after and violation lists) archived per episode under execution/scoring/*.json. The scoring rule in this run was full_intent_constraint_validation; no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes (repair_provider_trace = null for the sampled confirmatory episodes).

Confirmatory analysis: paired_binary_analysis_v1 assembled a 2×2 paired contingency table of SAFE outcomes across the two arms for the preregistered adversarial cluster and computed an exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value with paired bootstrap CI. All analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis logs) are archived and immutable.
sections.results:
Execution summary and raw outcomes: The run completed all planned episodes: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Model call accounting: model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task) versus preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 (one independent generation per arm). The per‑condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1), yielding observed SAFE rates of 1.0 for both arms.

Paired contingency and inferential result: The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline, SAFE encoding) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). These precise values were computed by the preregistered analysis executor and are archived (analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts above).

Representative artifact diagnostics: Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-00000X-*.json) show that shared_initial_candidate content was identical for baseline and guarded arms in every inspected confirmatory example; validator_traces for these episodes report violation_count = 0 and valid = true in validation_before and validation_after blocks. No repair_provider_trace entries were present in the sampled confirmatory scoring files, confirming that the guarded pipeline did not exercise the repair path under the executed sample.

Sensitivity and missingness: The preregistered missingness plan allowed automated retry logic and exclusions; execution logs record zero technical failures and zero exclusions (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). The exploratory reserve (up to 50 diagnostic tasks) was unused in the confirmatory analysis; exploratory ROC estimation remains available in the archive for later repeats that intentionally trigger verifier refusals.
sections.discussion:
Why the experiment was non‑informative for the causal estimand: Three artifact‑grounded choices combined to produce a ceiling effect that prevented detection of verifier benefit. First, shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) meant each pair received an identical LLM candidate; with identical candidates, the only possible discordance arises from post‑generation repair in the guarded arm, but no repairs occurred in the confirmatory episodes. Second, on the sampled tasks and against gpt‑5‑mini, the generated candidates satisfied the deterministic validator—observed baseline unsafe rate = 0%—so no unsafe proposals existed to be blocked by the verifier. Third, the model_call budget realized during execution (model_calls_used = 200) did not allocate the additional ~200 LLM calls that independent per‑arm generation would have required. The conjunction of identical per‑pair candidates and zero baseline violations yields n10 = n01 = 0 and a degenerate McNemar configuration (n11 = 200), producing a p‑value of 1.0 and CI [0,0]. All of these facts are verifiable in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json.

Implications for evaluation design: This run illustrates that preregistration options must be selected with awareness of their causal implications. Allowing shared_initial_candidate as an option is defensible for resource‑limited exploratory work, but when testing a paired causal estimand about verifier impact, independent per‑arm generation is the necessary default because it permits per‑arm variability and allows the guarded pipeline to act on differing proposals. For our N=200 design, independent per‑arm generation requires approximately 200 additional LLM calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400). If resource constraints preclude independent generation, alternative estimands (e.g., within‑arm absolute unsafe rates with repeated independent draws) or targeted injection of adversarial unsafe candidates should be preregistered to ensure testability.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats (concrete): (1) Use independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task). For our design this means allocating model_calls ≈ 400 rather than 200. (2) Strengthen adversarial coverage by reserving a calibrated fraction of tasks for injected unsafe patterns (templated obfuscations, negations, contradictory requirements) so that baseline unsafe rates are nonzero under the target model; record and preregister the injection fraction. (3) Use the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to estimate verifier ROC (true‑positive and false‑positive rates) and report CIs. (4) Consider modest multi‑model panels if resource budgets permit to evaluate generality across model families. These recommendations are directly supported by the archived preregistration and execution accounting records.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for gpt‑5‑mini, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (a) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts that permit exact replay; (b) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (c) we provide concrete, archived recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting, model‑call accounting) to design informative repeats. The archived execution and analysis bundle (execution/* and analysis/*) is provided to support deterministic replays and community replication.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in sandboxed synthetic states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
